Describe the stores you want
Your agent can only find what you describe. A vague ideal customer brings vague stores; a precise one brings shops where your products already make sense. Here is what to write.

A weak description and a strong one
Too vague
Shops that sell kids’ clothes.
Your agent can use this

Independent children’s boutiques with a shop front and a website, selling clothing for ages 0 to 6 in natural fabrics, at mid to premium prices. No department stores, no discount chains, no shops that only sell second hand. Like these three: [three shops you admire].

The second one tells the agent the kind of store, the niche, the price level, what to leave out and what a good match looks like. Every store it finds then comes with a line that says why it fits, so you can see at once whether the description is working.
The fields, one by one
Store type. Boutique, gift shop, pet store, outdoor store, wholesaler. This also decides which specialist agent takes the job.
Niche. What they focus on: organic baby clothes, handmade home goods, premium dog treats.
Area. The country of the agent, and, if you want, the states, provinces or cities that matter to you.
Size. Single shops, small groups of two to ten stores, or larger.
Signs that a store fits. Things you could see on their website: they stock similar brands, they sell at your price level, they mention “local makers”.
Exclusions. What the agent must never propose: chains, marketplaces, competitors, a region you already cover with a distributor.
Three to five example stores. The most useful field of all. Real shops you would love to be in teach the agent your taste better than any description.
One ideal customer per kind of store

If you sell to two very different kinds of shops, say gift shops and garden centres, do not mix them in one description. Create two ideal customers: each gets its own specialist, its own search and its own email, and the report shows you which one works better.

The fastest way to understand StockistScout is to follow one business from the first question to the first reply. Here is a made-up example, with every step the app really takes.

Example with a fictional business

Meet Clay & Fern, a small ceramics studio. They make mugs, bowls and vases by hand, they sell some online, and they want more gift and home shops to carry their work. They have tried sending emails themselves: it takes hours to find the right shops, and most messages never get an answer.
This is what happens when they give the job to an agent.
1. They describe the business, the customer and the offer
The setup is a questionnaire in three parts. It is detailed on purpose, because everything the agent does later comes from it.
Your business: what they sell (handmade stoneware mugs, bowls and vases), their website, their best sellers and their wholesale price range.

Your ideal customer: independent gift, home and décor shops that carry handmade or local products, with a website, in the United States; no big chains and no discount stores. They add three shops they would love to be in, as examples.

Your offer: a $250 opening order, payment on invoice after the first order, no samples but a small trial assortment, free shipping on the first order, and the next step they want: “reply and we send the wholesale catalogue”.
At the end of each part, Katya, the setup coach, reads what they wrote and suggests improvements field by field. She never invents a price or a discount: if a fact is missing, she asks for it.
2. The right specialist takes the job

Each kind of store has its own agent. Gift and home shops belong to Elias, so Elias takes Clay & Fern’s ideal customer: his own search, his own emails and his own report on the dashboard. A brand that sells to two kinds of stores, say gift shops and garden centres, uses two ideal customers and gets two agents.
3. The agent finds stores, and says why each one fits

Elias searches the web for shops that match the description and checks each one: what it sells, where it is, whether it has a business email it publishes, and whether it is a chain or one of the shops Clay & Fern excluded. Most candidates are discarded on purpose. Every store he keeps comes with one line that says why it fits.
Stores contacted: each store, why it fits and what happened next. A sample account with fictional stores.
Stores are approved automatically. If Clay & Fern prefer to approve each store themselves, they switch that on, and the shops they reject are never proposed again.
4. One reviewed template, a different email for each store

Before anything goes out, the email template is reviewed. An AI checks that it is honest, that it promises nothing the facts do not support, that it carries a real sender, a postal address and an opt-out, and that it does not read like spam. A template that needs changes comes back with notes, and “Fix it with Katya” proposes how to solve each one.

From that approved template, Elias writes each shop its own email, and mentions what makes that shop a good place for handmade ceramics. It goes out under Clay & Fern’s name, with their email as the reply-to.
5. Sending, a little more each week

A new sender that sends a lot at once ends up in spam. So every account starts at 25 emails a day and rises 50% each week after a healthy week, up to 500 a day per sending domain. Clay & Fern chose Plus, 1,000 emails a month, which the ramp reaches in its second week.

Your business can be anywhere. Your agent works the country you choose, finds stores there and writes to them in their language. Here is how that looks for a manufacturer that wants its first stores in the United States.
7 min read

Lin runs a family factory that makes stoneware plates and bowls. For years they sold through import agents and trade fairs. Now they want to sell directly to independent kitchen, gift and home shops in the United States, where their products would sit next to brands that cost three times more. The problem is the usual one: how do you find hundreds of the right shops on the other side of the world, and how do you write to them in a way they read?
Set it up in your own language

Lin fills in the setup in Chinese: the app and the setup coach speak sixteen languages. What changes is the country of each agent. Lin chooses the United States, so the agent searches US shops and writes to them in English, while every screen, report and suggestion stays in Chinese for Lin.
Ideal customer: independent kitchenware, gift and home shops in the United States that sell tableware, with a website and a business email; no chains, no discount stores.
Example stores: three US shops Lin would love to be in.
Offer: a $300 opening order, prices in US dollars, shipped from their US warehouse in 5 to 7 days, payment by card or invoice.
An offer that works across a border

A US shop owner who gets an email from a factory abroad has three questions before anything else: what does it cost delivered, how long does it take, and who handles a problem. The offer should answer them before they are asked.
Price in their currency, delivered. Quote in US dollars and say whether shipping and import duties are included. “Duties paid, delivered to your door” removes the biggest worry.
A small first order. A new stockist does not risk a container. A low opening minimum, with a bigger discount for larger orders, gets the first “yes”.
Real delivery times. Stock in the country ships in days; from the factory it can take weeks. Say which one applies, honestly.
The rules of their market. Products for children, food contact or cosmetics have their own requirements in each country. Have the documents ready, and say so only if you have them.
A person who answers. Replies come to your email. Answer within a day, in their language and in their working hours.
What the numbers look like

Lin picks Growth, 2,000 emails a month. A new sender cannot send that many from the first day, so sending climbs week by week: about 1,640 emails can go out in the first month, and the full 2,000 from the second. Each shop that fits gets its own email, and a follow-up a week later if it does not answer; both count as emails. So in the first month well over a thousand US shops hear about Lin’s factory.

How many of those shops answer, and how many buy, is not something anyone can promise: it depends on the product, the price, the offer and how quickly Lin answers. As simple arithmetic, if 1 shop in 50 replied, a thousand shops would mean about 20 conversations in the first month. Lin’s real numbers will be on the dashboard every day, per agent: sent, opened, clicked and replied.
Arithmetic, not a promise. The reply rate above is only an assumption to show the scale. Your own rate can be higher or lower; the Reports page shows it as it happens.

A wholesale email store buyers answer

Store owners get pitches every day. Most are long, generic and full of claims, and they go unread. The ones that get answers are short, specific and easy to reply to. Here is the difference, with an example.
Before: the pitch nobody answers
Before
Subject: The #1 eco brand your customers are begging for!!!

Dear Sir/Madam, we are the leading sustainable brand in the industry, loved by thousands of customers worldwide. Our products will boost your sales by 40%. Check our full catalogue, our Instagram, our TikTok and our website, and order now to get our exclusive limited-time discount!

Everything in it works against a reply: a subject that looks like spam, a greeting to nobody, claims the buyer cannot check, a promise of sales nobody can make, four links and a push to order before any conversation.
After: short, specific, one question
After
Subject: Handmade mugs for your shop

Hi Maya, I saw that your shop carries pottery from local makers, and the speckled glazes on your shelf are close to what we make at our studio: stoneware mugs and bowls, made by hand in small batches.
Would you like to see our wholesale catalogue and prices?
Ana, Clay & Fern
It is about her shop, not about us. It says why the products fit there. It asks one question that is easy to answer with “yes”. And it does not try to sell in the first message.
Why your agent starts with a short letter

That is exactly how StockistScout writes. The first email from your agent is a short letter: it introduces your business, says why it fits that store and asks one question, with no prices and no list of links. When the store answers, your agent sends your full email right away in the same conversation, with your photos, your best sellers and your offer, and forwards the reply to you. If the store says no, it never hears from you again.
A short letter that a busy owner reads in ten seconds.
The store answers, and the reply comes to you as well.
Your full email, with photos, products and your offer, arrives in the same thread.
You take it from there: the conversation and the order are yours.
Short letters also reach the inbox more often than heavy designed emails from a sender the store does not know yet, which matters as much as the words.
What the review checks before anything is sent

No template sends until it passes review. An AI reads every new or edited template and approves it, sends it back with the changes needed, or passes it to a person on our team when in doubt. It checks that:
it is honest: no false claims, no promises you cannot keep, nothing your offer does not say;
it uses no other companies’ brands or names;
it carries a real sender, a postal address and a way to unsubscribe;
nothing in it reads like spam.
Reports: sent, opened, clicked and replied, per day and per agent. A sample account.
Test two versions and keep the winner

You can run a version B with another angle, a different subject or a different first line, against your first email. The Reports page shows which one gets more replies, and you keep that one. A follow-up goes a week later to stores that did not answer, and that is the last email they get.

What to put in your wholesale offer
A store buyer who reads about a new brand wants to know, in a few seconds, whether it is worth a reply. Five short answers decide it. Here they are, with examples.

In StockistScout the offer is its own part of the setup, and its answers go into every email your agent writes. The review also checks them: an email can only promise what your offer says. So it pays to get them right once.
1. Minimum order
The first question of every buyer: how much do I have to commit? A low opening order gets more first orders; you can ask for more on reorders.
Good: “Opening order from $150, reorders from $100.”
Good: “12 pieces per style, mix and match across the collection.”
Costs replies: “MOQ 500 units per SKU” to a small boutique.
2. Payment terms
Say how and when they pay. Independent stores like to pay by card for a first order, and many expect payment terms once they reorder.
“First order by card; Net 30 from the second order.”
“Order on our wholesale site, or on a wholesale marketplace with its own terms.”
3. Samples
Be clear either way. If you send samples, say how many and whether they are free. If you do not, offer a way to judge the quality without risk.
“Free sample of two best sellers for stores with a shop front.”
“No samples, but your opening order can be as small as six pieces.”
4. An opening offer
A reason to say yes this month. Keep it simple, true and easy to check.
“Free shipping on your first order.”
“10% off the opening order.”
“Free shipping in the United States on orders of $1,000 or more.”

Only what is true. The setup coach never invents a discount, and the review stops any email that promises more than your offer says. If you do not have an opening offer, say nothing rather than something vague.
5. The next step
Tell the buyer exactly what to do: reply for the catalogue, open a wholesale account, or book a call. One step, not three. Your agent ends every email with it, and its button goes where you say.
Put it together
This is what a complete offer looks like, written the way you would answer the questionnaire:
A complete offer

Opening order from $150, reorders from $100. First order by card, Net 30 after that. No samples: the opening order can be six pieces. Free shipping on your first order. Reply and we send the wholesale catalogue and price list.
Five lines, and the buyer knows everything needed to decide whether to answer. Add your best sellers from your store, and every email shows a few of them as a sample of what you sell.
